items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A finite, ordered sequence of unambiguous instructions that solves a problem or completes a task"?
options: dry run
simulation
heuristic
algorithm
items.answer: algorithm
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of algorithm.

items.stem: Explain how pattern recognition leads to more efficient code.
items.answer: Recognising that steps repeat lets the programmer write them once – as a loop or a reusable function with parameters – rather than duplicating code, which reduces errors and simplifies maintenance.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Recognising that steps repeat lets the programmer write them once – as a loop or a reusable function with parameters – rather than duplicating code, which reduces errors and simplifies maintenance. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Noah writes: "Abstraction means making a problem more complicated so that it is more realistic." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Abstraction means hiding or removing unnecessary detail to simplify the problem.
items.markingKey: Abstraction means hiding or removing unnecessary detail to simplify the problem. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Identify the computational thinking concept that is mainly shown in each case: (a) A recipe app breaks "cook dinner" into shopping list, preparation steps and cooking timers. (b) An engineer writes precise numbered steps for resetting a router so that anyone can follow them. (c) A weather app shows only temperature, rain chance and wind for each hour, ignoring air pressure details.
items.answer: (a) decomposition; (b) algorithm design; (c) abstraction
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: (a) decomposition; (b) algorithm design; (c) abstraction.

items.stem: A loop produces the values 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, … Use pattern recognition to give a general rule for the n-th value and state the 20th value. Explain how generalising the rule helps the programmer.
items.markingKey: Rule T(n) = n(n + 1)/2 (2); T(20) = 210 (1); a general formula/function works for any n, avoiding special-case code (1).

items.stem: A city council in Medellín wants an app to help residents plan journeys combining buses, metro and cable cars. Apply decomposition, pattern recognition and abstraction to the design of this app.
items.answer: Decomposition: route finding, timetable data, user interface, ticket pricing, real-time updates, accessibility. Pattern recognition: each transport mode is a network of stops and connections with times – one graph model; journey cost follows the same calculation per leg. Abstraction: represent stops as nodes and connections as weighted edges (time, cost), ignoring street detail, vehicle type or exact geography; keep only data relevant to planning.
items.markingKey: Decomposition: route finding, timetable data, user interface, ticket pricing, real-time updates, accessibility. Pattern recognition: each transport mode is a network of stops and connections with times – one graph model; journey cost follows the same calculation per leg. Abstraction: represent stops as nodes and connections as weighted edges (time, cost), ignoring street detail, vehicle type or exact geography; keep only data relevant to planning.

items.stem: "Computational thinking is only useful for computer scientists." Discuss.
items.answer: Computational thinking is a general problem-solving approach valuable far beyond computer science.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it underpins programming and system design. Arguments against: decomposition, abstraction and pattern recognition are used in science, business planning, medicine and everyday problem solving. Supported judgement: Computational thinking is a general problem-solving approach valuable far beyond computer science. Markbands (6 marks): top band: well-balanced discussion with accurate, specific technical detail applied to the context and a justified conclusion; middle band: some balance and correct terminology, conclusion only partly supported; bottom band: descriptive, largely one-sided, little technical detail or application.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "abstraction"?
options: The diamond-shaped flowchart symbol for a yes/no question, with one arrow leaving for each outcome
Removing unnecessary detail and focusing on the essential features of a problem in order to model it
Designing a clear, step-by-step solution that can be followed by a computer or a person
The control structure in which instructions are executed one after another in order
items.answer: Removing unnecessary detail and focusing on the essential features of a problem in order to model it
items.markingKey: B. "abstraction" is removing unnecessary detail and focusing on the essential features of a problem in order to model it.

items.stem: Explain why abstraction is essential when creating a computer model of a real system.
items.answer: Real systems contain far more detail than can be represented or computed; abstraction keeps only the features that affect the result, making the model simpler, faster to build and easier to understand.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Real systems contain far more detail than can be represented or computed; abstraction keeps only the features that affect the result, making the model simpler, faster to build and easier to understand. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between abstraction and decomposition.
items.answer: Decomposition splits a problem into smaller parts; abstraction removes unnecessary details to focus on what matters. They are often used together.
items.markingKey: Decomposition splits a problem into smaller parts; abstraction removes unnecessary details to focus on what matters. They are often used together. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
The following algorithm is written in pseudocode.
MARKS ← [80, 56, 60, 50]
TOTAL ← 0
PASS ← 0
loop I from 0 to 3
    TOTAL ← TOTAL + MARKS[I]
    if MARKS[I] >= 50 then
        PASS ← PASS + 1
    end if
end loop
output TOTAL / 4, PASS
State the output and describe the purpose of the algorithm.
items.answer: Output: 61.5, 4. Purpose: it calculates the mean mark and the number of passes.
items.markingKey: Output 61.5, 4 (2 marks; 1 for a partially correct trace); purpose: calculates the mean mark and the number of passes (1).

items.markingKey: Pseudocode is not executed; it must be clear and consistent, but small syntax variations are acceptable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Design, in pseudocode, an algorithm that reads the ages of visitors to a museum until −1 is entered, then outputs the number of child (under 12), adult and senior (65+) visitors and the total ticket income (child 5, adult 15, senior 8). Explain how your algorithm uses sequence, selection and iteration.
items.answer: Initialise counters C, A, S ← 0; input AGE; loop while AGE ≠ −1: if AGE < 12 then C ← C + 1 else if AGE >= 65 then S ← S + 1 else A ← A + 1 end if; input AGE; end loop; output C, A, S, 5C + 15A + 8S. Sequence: initialisation then loop then output; selection: classifying each age; iteration: the sentinel-controlled loop.
items.markingKey: Initialise counters C, A, S ← 0; input AGE; loop while AGE ≠ −1: if AGE < 12 then C ← C + 1 else if AGE >= 65 then S ← S + 1 else A ← A + 1 end if; input AGE; end loop; output C, A, S, 5C + 15A + 8S. Sequence: initialisation then loop then output; selection: classifying each age; iteration: the sentinel-controlled loop.

items.markingKey: Decompose: collect addresses/needs, assign households to vans, order stops, print route sheets. Abstraction: graph of addresses (nodes) and travel times (weighted edges); ignore exact street layouts and van details. Pattern: same process every day → reusable program. Algorithm: exact routing is infeasible (TSP), so use a heuristic – cluster by area then nearest-neighbour ordering, possibly improved with 2-opt; check van capacity constraints. Test with real data and refine.
